::: {.chapter-goal}
#### In this chapter
You will tour every panel of the Code Editor, run your first script, read a global elevation model, and learn the three diagnostic habits that will save you more time than any other technique in this book.
:::

## Two front doors

Earth Engine offers two ways in, and choosing correctly at the start saves a lot of frustration.

The **Explorer** is a point and click catalogue browser. You search a dataset, add it to a map, adjust the stretch, and export. There is no code. For checking whether a dataset covers your area, or for showing a colleague what Sentinel-2 looks like over their district, it is the fastest tool available. It is also where a non technical stakeholder can be left alone safely.

The **Code Editor** is where this book lives. Everything reproducible, everything automatable, and everything beyond a handful of operations happens here. The trade is a scripting language, which Chapter [-@sec-javascript] covers from zero.

::: {.callout-tip}
## In practice
Use the Explorer for reconnaissance, then move to the Code Editor to build. The reverse order, discovering in month two that your chosen dataset has a three month gap over your study area, is a preventable and common waste.
:::

## The four panels

Open [code.earthengine.google.com](https://code.earthengine.google.com). The interface divides into four regions, and each maps to a distinct stage of work.

**Left, the library.** Three tabs. *Scripts* holds your code repositories, backed by Git, which means your work is versioned and shareable by link. *Docs* is the complete API reference, searchable, and worth using in preference to a web search because it always matches the deployed version. *Assets* holds data you have uploaded: shapefiles of study boundaries, training polygons, rasters from other sources.

**Centre, the editor.** Your script. Above it sit **Run**, which executes, **Save**, and **Get Link**, which produces a URL reproducing the exact script for anyone who opens it. That link is the standard way Earth Engine work is shared in papers and reports.

**Right, the feedback loop.** Three tabs, and this is where your attention should sit while learning. *Console* receives everything you `print()`, including charts and full object descriptions. *Inspector* turns the map into a query tool: click any pixel and read its value in every band of every visible layer. *Tasks* holds pending exports to Drive, Cloud Storage or Assets.

**Bottom, the map.** Not merely output. The drawing tools in the top left corner create geometries directly, which appear in an *Imports* block at the top of your script. That is how training polygons get drawn in Chapter [-@sec-sampling].

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common failure: the Imports block that does not travel
Geometries drawn on the map, and datasets added with the Import button, are stored in the Imports block above your code. When you copy a script into an email or a document, that block is usually left behind. The recipient gets an undefined variable error on line one. Either define geometries in code, as this book does, or share by **Get Link**, which carries the imports.
:::

## Reading the reply

The interesting part is not the map. It is the Console.

When you expand the printed object, you see Earth Engine describing what it holds: the image type, a list of bands with their data types and pixel dimensions, and a block of metadata properties. Three things in that reply matter more than the rest.

**Band names.** `elevation` here, but `B4` on Sentinel-2, `SR_B4` on Landsat Collection 2, `VV` on Sentinel-1. Guessing band names is the leading cause of the phrase "this layer does not exist" appearing in your Console.

**Data type.** SRTM elevation is a signed 16 bit integer. That matters the moment you divide it, because integer division truncates. Chapter [-@sec-indices] returns to this when indices start producing suspicious zeroes.

**Projection and scale.** Every band carries a native pixel size. When you combine bands of different sizes, Earth Engine resolves the conflict by rules that are documented but easy to forget, and the result can silently resample your ten metre data to ninety metres.

## Three habits worth forming now

These are not stylistic preferences. Each one prevents a category of error that is otherwise very hard to diagnose.

**Print early, print often.** After every meaningful step, print the result and look at it. Lazy evaluation means an error made now surfaces much later, and by then the cause is invisible. A print statement is how you force evaluation on your own schedule.

**Check collection sizes before proceeding.** `print('scenes:', collection.size())` after each filter chain. An empty collection does not raise an error at the point it becomes empty. It raises a confusing one twenty lines later.

**Use the Inspector against your intuition.** When a classification looks wrong, click on a misclassified pixel and read every predictor value. Nine times out of ten the reason is visible immediately: a band is masked, a value is on the wrong scale, or a cloud survived masking.

::: {.callout-note}
## Concept: `shown` and `opacity`
`Map.addLayer()` takes five arguments, and the last two are underused. Adding a layer with `shown` set to `0` registers it in the Layers control without cluttering the map, which lets you build up a dozen diagnostic layers and flick between them. `opacity` at `0.5` over a basemap is the fastest way to check whether a classification aligns with visible features on the ground.
:::

## A note on assets and quotas

Your Assets tab is personal storage, roughly 250 gigabytes on a free account. Uploads accept shapefiles, GeoTIFFs and CSV point files. Two operational habits are worth adopting from the start.

Give assets descriptive identifiers, because `projects/your-project/assets/mangrove_training_2023_v2` will still make sense in eighteen months and `asset1` will not. And expect uploads to be slow relative to everything else on the platform, since this is the one direction in which you are still moving data.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Run the script, then use the Inspector to find the elevation of the highest point within your own country's borders. Compare it to the published figure and account for any difference.
2. Change `max` from 1200 to 3000, rerun, and write one sentence on what information the map gains and what it loses.
3. Search the Docs tab for `ee.Terrain.slope`. Add a slope layer to the script without looking ahead to Chapter [-@sec-terrain].
4. Save the script to a repository and generate a **Get Link** URL. Open it in a private browser window to confirm it reproduces cleanly.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

**1.** For Indonesia the published summit is Puncak Jaya (Carstensz Pyramid), 4,884 m. The Inspector will show a lower value on the highest SRTM pixel. Reasons: each pixel is an average over 30 m (or 90 m), so a sharp summit is smoothed down; SRTM was acquired in 2000 by radar, which has voids and errors on steep, icy peaks; and the published height uses a different vertical datum and survey. A difference of tens of metres is expected and is a lesson about what a pixel is, not an error in your script.

**2.** With `max: 3000` the colour ramp is stretched over a larger range, so mountains are no longer saturated at the top colour and you can see differences between 1,500 and 3,000 m. In exchange, lowlands below a few hundred metres collapse into nearly one colour, so detail in coastal plains and deltas is lost. The stretch decides which part of the data you can see; choose it for the question.

**3.**

```javascript
var slope = ee.Terrain.slope(dem);           // degrees, computed from the DEM
Map.addLayer(slope, {min: 0, max: 45, palette: ['white', 'orange', 'brown']}, 'Slope');
```
`ee.Terrain.slope` needs an elevation image in metres and returns slope in degrees. If your layer is all white, check that you passed the DEM and not a visualised copy of it.

**4.** A clean result opens the script with no undefined-variable error and draws the same layers. If it fails in the private window, the usual causes are a geometry drawn on the map that was not saved with the link (open **Get Link** after saving), or an asset that is private: share it or make it readable by anyone with the link.
:::
